beliefs.practice: Read the cluster connection string from an environment variable (DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never hard-code it; create a single AsyncIOMotorClient per process and reuse it for all Beanie/ODM operations (close it on shutdown).
Enable TLS/SSL on the Mongo client connection (tls=true) and verify server certificates; do not disable certificate verification in production.
Tune Mongo client pool and timeouts: set a sensible maxPoolSize for expected concurrency and configure serverSelectionTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS to avoid long blocking calls.
Store secrets (DOCUMENTDB_URI, OPENAI_API_KEY) in environment variables or a secrets store; never commit keys to source control and provide a .env.example placeholder file.
Avoid logging or printing the full connection string or API keys; redact sensitive fields if connection strings must be shown in logs.
Use a single durable unique key for each review (review_id or _id) and create a unique index on it to make upserts idempotent (use update_one/replace_one with upsert=True).

Model sentiment as a numeric field (e.g., sentiment_score float normalized to -1..1 or 0..1) and store tags as a small array of strings (tags: ["feature", "delivery"]). Index sentiment or tags selectively based on query patterns.
Keep document sizes small (well below 2 MB); store large assets externally (blob storage) and keep references in the document to reduce RU cost and avoid item-size limits.

Create indexes to support your aggregation/reporting: at minimum index product_id and sentiment (or a compound index on (product_id, sentiment)) to accelerate GROUP BY product+sentiment aggregation pipelines.
Avoid unnecessary indexes (each index increases RU cost and storage); measure index usage and drop unused indexes. Create sparse or partial indexes when appropriate to reduce index size.

If using vector search, declare the vector field with its dimensionality and create a vector index specifying algorithm (e.g., hnsw or ivf), metric (cosine/inner_product), and tuning parameters (M, efConstruction, nlist, efSearch) appropriate for recall/latency tradeoffs.
When performing vector queries, project only required fields and limit the number of returned neighbors; use efSearch or query-time parameters to balance accuracy and RU/latency.

Implement retries with exponential backoff for transient errors (network errors, 429 throttling, transient 5xx responses); detect rate-limiting responses and respect Retry-After headers where provided.

Provision throughput to avoid throttling: use autoscale RU/s or database/container-level provisioned throughput sized for peak ingestion and aggregation workloads; monitor RU consumption and scale proactively.

Design aggregation pipelines to be RU-efficient: project early ($project), filter early ($match), avoid $lookup where possible, and use $group on indexed fields when feasible; test pipeline RU cost with real data.
Use pagination and batching for reads/queries (limit + skip or range queries with sort) to avoid scanning large collections in a single request; tune batchSize for cursor iteration.

Instrument and monitor RU usage, latency, request charges, index metrics, and slow queries; integrate with Azure monitoring/alerts and collect logs/metrics from MCP server tools for index/query plans.

Limit concurrency when calling external services (OpenAI): use an async semaphore to bound simultaneous requests so you do not overwhelm the network or exceed throughput limits for the pipeline or the database.

Use idempotent processing: design the enrichment pipeline so that re-processing the same review (e.g., via upsert with a stable key) produces the same result and does not create duplicates or partial writes.

Define JSON schema validation on the collection (if supported) or validate in the application layer to ensure required fields (product_id, review_text) and types (sentiment_score numeric, tags array) before writing to the DB.
When using Beanie ODM, declare indexes in the Document Settings and call init_beanie once at app startup with the database object rather than creating indexes ad-hoc on each request.
Avoid expensive text-search indexes unless required; prefer extracting structured tags/key themes (via OpenAI) and indexing those tags for fast filtering and aggregation instead of free-text queries.

Test the pipeline end-to-end with a mock OpenAI implementation and deterministic seeds so CI runs do not require real API keys; allow switching to real OpenAI via configuration only when running in a controlled environment.

Use database-level or container-level throughput grouping: collocate related collections/documents under the same partition key (e.g., product_id) to optimize hot partitions and RU distribution; choose partition key with high cardinality.
Plan for backups and retention: enable built-in continuous or periodic backup and test restore procedures; for critical data, export periodic snapshots to durable storage.
